Both heads are covered with animal skin or a synthetic head, the treble head often being plastic or synthetic; the heads are tensioned with braided rope or with nuts and bolts, so the pitch can be adjusted. The beaters are mostly wood or rattan, the traditional bass beater being a naturally curved branch of hardwood such as oak or mahogany, and the treble beater thinner and springier. The strap is usually braided cotton, and in some regions the drum is also struck with bamboo sticks.
卓爾鼓屬南亞雙面膜鳴鼓。Shail Vyas 認為，它可能受印度河流域文明發現的: The dhol is a double-headed membranophone of South Asia. Shail Vyas suggests that it may have been influenced by a similar clay instrument found in the Indus Valley civilisation. Early Indian sculpture already sets the dhol beside the tabla as a leading percussion instrument. Documents record the dhol in the ensemble of the Mughal emperor Akbar. The Indo-European word 'dhol' appears in writing around 1800, in the Sangitasara. The chronicles of Assam show that the dhol was present there by the fourteenth century at the latest, played by local people. After electronic equipment such as the tape recorder appeared, the standing of dhol players at celebrations declined, though the drum is still heard on recordings.
卓爾鼓常見於南亞婚禮遊行、卡瓦里（Qawwali）音樂與地方歌舞伴奏，也出現在旁: The dhol is common in wedding processions across South Asia, in Qawwali music and as accompaniment to regional song and dance. It also appears in Punjabi Sufi ritual, in the Bihu dance of Rangali Bihu at the Assamese new year, in the Shigmo festival and temple-fair music of Goa, in the garba dance of Gujarat's Navaratri festival, in the drum troupes of Maharashtra's Ganesh festival, and in the Dollu Kunitha folk dance of Karnataka. In modern stage bhangra and in recordings of Punjabi pop songs it, or a related double-headed drum, plays rhythms such as kahwa.
卓爾鼓擁有渾厚而富有穿透力的音色，兼具溫暖與力量感。其雙面設計使得鼓聲具有明顯的: The dhol has a full, penetrating timbre that is both warm and powerful. Its two heads give the sound a marked low-frequency resonance, and its range is wide, covering everything from a deep bass up into the middle register. A stroke sets rich overtones moving in the skin, producing a clearly layered resonance that is neither too sharp nor too dull, with both brightness and weight. Compared with the Western bass drum, the dhol sounds more distinctly regional, warm without losing its outline; compared with African drums, its sound carries further and travels clearly through a large outdoor celebration. That character makes it the soul instrument of the subcontinent's folk music and festivities.

The dhol is a double-headed barrel membranophone used widely across the Indian subcontinent, varying in size and material from place to place. The body is usually a wooden barrel, with animal skin or synthetic heads at both ends tensioned by rope or screws, the thick head giving low frequencies and the thin head high ones. The player strikes it with two wooden or rattan sticks, a thicker curved stick on the bass side and a thin one on the treble side, and the drum hangs from the shoulder or neck on a cotton strap. It is common in wedding processions and in religious and festival music, and it also appears in Punjab, Assam, Goa, Gujarat, Maharashtra and other regions.
卓爾鼓通常以棉織背帶斜掛於肩前，少數情況掛於頸部。演奏時使用兩根木製或藤製鼓棒：: The dhol usually hangs across the front of the body from a cotton strap over the shoulder, and in a few cases from the neck. It is played with two wooden or rattan beaters: the thicker one, slightly curved at the tip, strikes the thicker head and gives a solid low note, while the thinner, more pliable one strikes the thinner head and gives a high note. Begin by adjusting the heads with the rope or the screws, tighter for a higher pitch and looser for a lower one, then practise alternating between the two heads. In some regions the drum is also struck with bamboo sticks or with the hands.
